title: The unripe word
hook: without the True Guru, other words are unripe (Anand 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, nidhaan, and your line, treasure within. Today, a pauri about which words are worth keeping.

A fruit stall in Amritsar. A woman picks up a mango, presses it with her thumb, and puts it back. Kacha, she says. Unripe. She tries another that gives a little and smells sweet. Pakka. Ripe. Those two words run all through Punjabi and Hindi. A kacha road is dirt; a pakka road is paved. A kacha house is mud; a pakka house is brick. Kacha means not ready yet: not fired, not finished. Guru Amar Das took that market word and set it into the Anand.
screen: `A MANGO AT A FRUIT STALL.` → `KACHA: UNRIPE. PAKKA: RIPE.` → `A MARKET WORD IN THE ANAND.`

segments.voice: Pauri twenty-three calls out to the Sikhs of the True Guru: come and sing the true bani, the true word. Pauri twenty-four turns the coin over. Its refrain says, in paraphrase, that without the True Guru every other word is kachee, unripe. Then the circle widens. Those who say such words are unripe. Those who hear them are unripe. Those who explain them are unripe. Even someone who repeats the Lord's name all day may not understand a thing, if the mind has been carried off by maya, the pull of the passing world. So the problem isn't vocabulary; holy words can be said in an unripe way. The pauri points at two things: where a word comes from, and the mind that receives it. For Sikhs, the ripe word is gurbani, the Gurus' own words, gathered in the Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks that the kirtan sung in the congregation be gurbani, along with the writings of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. There's an everyday edge, too. Plenty of what gets said in a day is a little kacha: the half-heard rumor, the quick hot take, the reply typed before the message was finished. The pauri doesn't ask anyone to go silent. It asks whether a word has a true source, and whether it's ready.
screen: `KACHA: UNRIPE, UNFIRED, NOT READY.` · `PAURI 24: WITHOUT THE GURU, WORDS ARE RAW.` · `SPEAKER, HEARER, EXPLAINER: ALL UNRIPE.` · `RIPE: A TRUE SOURCE, A PRESENT MIND.` · then, large: `RIPE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let one sentence from the last day come up that was a little kacha: said too fast, half true, or said to win. Don't argue with it; just notice it, the way the woman at the stall feels the mango and sets it down, then rest with the breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, quietly, and let the rest be silence.

Kachee, unripe or raw. Kachee baanee: in the Anand, any word that doesn't come from the True Guru, or is said by a mind somewhere else. This week: bliss known through the Guru, given not grabbed, the narrow way, treasure within, and now ripe words.
Your line: ripe words. Some words need one more breath before they're ready. That's day three hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the full Anand Sahib in the morning, and pauri 24's warning about unripe words is often cited to explain why kirtan in the gurdwara is drawn from gurbani.

chat.says: Anand says some words are unripe. Does that just mean bad words, like swearing?
options: No: words without the True Guru are raw, and even holy words can be said unripely.
Yes, it's a list of rude words that Sikhs aren't allowed to say out loud at all.
It means any word that isn't in Punjabi, since only Punjabi words count as ripe.
chat.meaning: Pauri 24: without the True Guru, every other word is kachee, unripe; even repeating the Name means little if maya has carried the mind off.

Bhai Gurdas.meaning: an early Sikh writer whose verses may be sung in kirtan
